newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Philippines sees sustained higher GNP growth.
newsitem.headline: Philippines sees sustained higher GNP growth.

text.p: The Philippines' recent spurt in Gross National Product (GNP) growth will continue with lower inflation next year, Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said on Tuesday.
Some analysts' fears of the growth being like a bubble that was about to burst were unfounded, he said.

"It (the economy) is exhibiting a sustained growth rate that is accompanied by a lower inflation rate. Had that not been the case, I might be moved to agree with some observers who look at in those ways," he told Reuters in an interview in Melbourne.
De Ocampo is in Melbourne for Australia's National Trade and Investment Outlook conference.
He said he saw GNP growth rising from the upper end of the 6.5 percent to 7.5 percent range in calendar 1996 to over seven percent in 1997.
Inflation was likely to fall to about seven percent in 1997 from eight percent this year.
The Philippines posted 7.1 percent GNP growth in the nine months to September 30, up from 5.3 percent in the same period a year earlier.
De Ocampo said the growth was export and investment driven.
Concern about growth being propped up by remittances from workers overseas related to worries about the trade deficit, he said.
He said the Philippines' trade deficit was not high compared with other developing countries and there had been some large special purchases such as aircraft recently.
The Philippines also did not include service exports in its figures, which tended to exaggerate the deficit.
De Ocampo also said he was confident credit ratings agencies would look at upgrading the Philippines sovereign ratings in the next year.
He referred to a recent Merrill Lynch report which said the Philippines could expect a credit rating upgrade very soon if it passed controversial tax reforms.
New taxes on beer and cigarettes were signed into law late last month and are expected to raise six billion to 6.5 billion pesos extra every year.

"Now it's passed, I wouldn't be surprised if the credit rating agencies come trooping back to Manila this coming year, because the country would have at the end of the year shown it's on a sustained growth path and by this time next year we would have exited the IMF for the first time in 30 years," he said.
A three-year International Monetary Fund (IMF) supervisory programme which set a range of goals is due to end in June 1997 and the Philippines has already met most of these goals.

"All of this points very forcefully to a credit upgrade," he said, adding that international investors had already made their judgements by pricing Philippine debt instruments at investment grade levels.
In February this year Moody's Investor Services upgraded the Philippines' long term foreign currency loan rating to Ba2 from Ba3, while Standard & Poors Corp raised its rating to BB from BB minus.
